title: Mark Twain: 'The Report of My Death Was an Exaggeration' (1897)
summary: In May 1897, when American newspapers erroneously printed sensational obituaries declaring that he had died in poverty in London, Mark Twain sent his legendary single-sentence correction.
keywords: Mark Twain: 'The Report of My Death Was an Exaggeration'
full_text:
In May 1897, while living in London to escape financial entanglements following the bankruptcy of his publishing house, Mark Twain was the subject of wild transatlantic rumors. A cousin, James Ross Clemens, had fallen seriously ill in London, leading careless correspondents to assume that the great humorist himself was near death.

On June 1, 1897, the New York Journal ran a sensational dispatch reporting that Samuel L. Clemens (Mark Twain) was destitute, dying, and possibly already dead in an obscure London garret.

Frank Marshall White, a young American correspondent stationed in London, rushed to Twain’s residence in Chelsea to investigate the grim news.

Twain opened the front door himself, looking hale, energetic, and puffing serenely on his pipe. White, pale and trembling with relief, showed him the sensational American cable.

Twain read the morbid obituary with immense amusement. Handing White a fountain pen, Twain scribbled his immortal note to the New York editor:
"Dear Sir,
You may inform my American readers that the report of my death was an exaggeration!"

The single sentence was cabled across the Atlantic and reprinted in hundreds of newspapers across the globe, dissolving the national mourning into delighted laughter. Twain transformed a reckless media blunder into one of the most celebrated epigrams of literary history.

moral: Calm wit easily punctures sensational falsehoods; serene humor disarms premature panic and gossip.
moral_reflection: Treat sensational rumors with calm, humorous detachment.
